title: Spoken Turkish
seoTitle: Spoken Turkish and texting: napıyosun, kanka
intro: Turkish as people speak and text it differs from the written standard in regular, predictable ways. The r of `-(I)yor` falls away (*geliyo*), the future shrinks (*gelicem*), *bir* becomes *bi* and *ne yapıyorsun* becomes *napıyosun*. This unit teaches you to understand these forms and to use them where they belong, with friends and in messages, and to keep them out of anything formal. It also covers the informal words and texting abbreviations you will meet every day: *kanka*, *harbiden*, *slm*, *tşk*.

blocks.text: In everyday speech the r of `-(I)yor` is hardly pronounced, and in messages people often leave it out. The rule is simple: the r drops before a consonant and at the end of the word. With *ben*, *-yorum* shrinks further, to *-yom*.

rows.en: he, she or it is coming (written: geliyor)
we're coming (the r stays before a vowel)

blocks.text: **What stays the same.** Vowel harmony, the negative and the question particle work as usual: *gelmiyom* (I'm not coming), *biliyo musun?* (do you know?), *geliyo mu?* (is he coming?). The past continuous and the reported forms lose their r too: *geliyodu* (he was coming), *geliyomuş* (apparently he's coming). With *biz*, a vowel follows, so the r usually stays; *geliyoz* is very casual. With *sen*, *geliyosun* is the usual reduction; *geliyon* is very casual, and typical of the Aegean ([C2 unit 4](gp-dialect-features)).

**Ne yap-.** The question *ne yapıyorsun?* fuses into one word: *napıyosun?* (what are you doing?, also just **how are you?**). The same fusion gives *naptın?* (what did you do?, how did it go?) and *napıcan?* (what are you going to do?). Writing the apostrophe, *n'apıyosun*, is optional.

blocks.text: In fast speech even a careful speaker's *geliyor* sounds like *geliyo*. When you hear *-yo*, think *-yor*.
These spellings are for speech and for messages to friends. Everywhere else, including your answers in this course unless a task asks for speech, write `-(I)yor` in full.

sections.title: Gelicem, yapcaz: the future in speech

blocks.text: The future shrinks in two steps. First, the vowel of `-(y)AcAk` narrows to ı, i, u or ü, as the a and e of a stem do before `-(I)yor`; with *ben* and *biz*, the ğ and the vowel after it fall away: *geleceğim* → *gelicem*, *yapacağız* → *yapıcaz*. In faster speech the narrow vowel goes too: *gelcem*, *yapcaz*. [A2 unit 3](gp-future) gave you a first glimpse of this.

**Back vowels** give *a* in the ending: *yapacağım* → *yapıcam*, *yapcam*; *olacak* → *olucak*, *olcak*. **Stems ending in a vowel** narrow it: *söyleyeceğim* → *söylicem*, *diyeceğim* → *diycem*, as in the everyday opener *Bişey diycem* (listen, there's something I want to tell you). The **negative** keeps its m: *gelmeyeceğim* → *gelmicem*, *yapmayacağız* → *yapmıcaz*. The **question** is regular: *gelcek misin?*
**Napıcan?** In the question *ne yapacaksın?*, the ending often shrinks to *-cAn*: *napıcan?* (what are you going to do?), *ne zaman gelcen?* (when are you coming?).

What are you doing tonight?
I'm not coming, I'm really tired.
There's something I want to tell you, but don't be cross.
What's going to happen now?

blocks.text: *Gelicem* is to *geleceğim* what English **gonna** is to **going to**, or French **j'vais** to **je vais**: everyone says it, and nobody writes it in a letter.
Don't mix the two systems in one word: write *gelicem* or *geleceğim*, never *geliceğim*.
A few very frequent words have spoken forms of their own. You will hear them constantly, and see them in every casual message.

**Bi** is *bir* without stress. It is the *bir* of requests ([B2 unit 9](gp-softeners)): *Bi bakar mısın?* (could you take a look?), *Bi dakka!* (just a minute!), *Bi kahve içelim mi?* (shall we grab a coffee?). When *bir* means **one** and carries stress, it stays *bir*: *Bir çay, bir kahve* (one tea, one coffee).

**Baya** is the spoken *bayağı*, an adverb meaning **quite, rather, really**: *Film baya güzeldi* (the film was really good), *Baya bekledik* (we waited quite a while). Don't confuse it with the adjective *bayağı*, **vulgar, common**: *bayağı bir şaka* (a vulgar joke).

**Di mi?** closes a sentence the way **right?** does: *Yarın geliyosun, di mi?* (you're coming tomorrow, right?). **N'aber?** (what's up?) is the casual greeting; the answer is *İyi, senden n'aber?* or *İdare eder*.

items.en: Hi, how are you?
Just a sec, my phone's ringing.
You're coming tomorrow, right?
The film was really good.
Don't look at me like that!

blocks.text: Fillers from [B2 unit 9](gp-fillers), such as *şey*, *yani*, *işte* and *falan*, go hand in hand with these reductions. Together they make speech sound natural; in writing, leave both out.

sections.title: Kanka, harbiden, slm: informal words and texting

blocks.text: Among friends, especially younger ones, a set of informal words replaces the neutral ones. Use them only with people you say *sen* to, and who use them too: with anyone else they sound rude, or comic.

head: Informal
Neutral
Meaning and use
rows: buddy, mate; to and about a close friend, of either sex (from *kan kardeşi*, blood brother)
thanks; OK, fine; mostly between men
what's up?, is something wrong? (at an unexpected call or visit)

blocks.text: **Valla** is short for *vallahi*, an oath by God. In everyday speech it is simply emphasis, and people of every outlook use it: *Valla çok güzel olmuş!* (honestly, it's turned out really nice!). **Hayırdır**, literally **it's for the good**, asks what has happened when something unusual does: a call at midnight, a friend at your door: *Hayırdır, bu saatte neden arıyorsun?*

items.en: Hey mate, what's up? What are you up to?
Seriously? I never heard about it.
Honestly, I don't know, ask her.
What's wrong? Why are you calling at this hour?
The match was awesome!

blocks.text: These words signal closeness. *Kanka* to a teacher, *eyvallah* in an email to a manager or *tşk* to a stranger reads as disrespect. With people you don't know well, stay neutral ([B2 unit 9](gp-register-shift)).

sections.title: When to write it as it is said

blocks.text: Standard spelling is always correct; a spoken spelling is a choice, and it tells your reader something about you and about them. There is no official spelling of *geliyo* or *gelicem*: the TDK's rules describe the written standard, and people spell speech in different ways (*naber* or *n'aber*, *gelcem* or *gelicem*).

items: **Write it as it is said** in messages and chats with friends and family, in casual social-media posts, in dialogue in stories, comics and scripts when a character's voice matters, and when you quote someone word for word.

**Keep to the standard** in emails to people you don't know well, teachers, colleagues and officials; in anything for work or school; in forms, applications and documents; in the narration of a story, even when its dialogue is spoken; and in anything you would sign.

blocks.text: **What doesn't change, even in a quick message.** The question particle `mI` and the conjunction *dA* are written apart ([A1 unit 4](gp-question-mi), [A1 unit 4](gp-de-also)): *geliyo musun?*, *ben de geliyom*. Gluing `mI` to the verb, or writing *bende* for **me too**, is a spelling mistake, not a style.
**In literature.** Novelists keep the narration in the standard and may let characters speak as they would: *“Gelmiyom!” diye bağırdı.* Subtitles and the news keep the standard throughout.

blocks.text: Casual messages often drop capitals, punctuation and the Turkish letters too (*naber nasilsin*), especially on keyboards without them. Friends don't mind. In anything formal, ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü are not optional: *sınır* (border) and *sinir* (nerve) are different words.
Registers, forms of address, and formal letters.

summary: In speech the r of `-(I)yor` drops before a consonant and at the end of the word: *geliyo*, *geliyosun*, *geliyolar*; with *ben*, *geliyom*.
The spoken future narrows its vowel and drops ğ: *gelicem*, *yapıcaz*; faster, *gelcem*, *yapcaz*.
*Bi*, *bişey*, *n'aber*, *di mi?* and *baya* are the spoken *bir*, *bir şey*, *ne haber*, *değil mi?* and *bayağı*.
*Kanka*, *harbiden*, *valla*, *eyvallah* and texting abbreviations (*slm*, *tmm*, *tşk*, *kib*) are for close friends only.
Write it as it is said to friends and in dialogue; keep to the standard in anything formal, in narration and in anything you would sign.
Even in a casual message, `mI` and *dA* are written apart: *geliyo musun?*, *ben de*.
